knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

# Part A - Creating Data Frames

```{r}
## Question 1
## a. Create a data frame using the shoe size and height data.
## Save it as shoesize.csv.

shoes <- data.frame(
  Gender = c("Male", "Female", "Male", "Female", "Male",
             "Female", "Male", "Female", "Male", "Female",
             "Male", "Female", "Male", "Female", "Male",
             "Female", "Male", "Female", "Male", "Female"),
  ShoeSize = c(10, 7, 11, 8, 12, 6, 10, 7, 11, 8,
               13, 6, 12, 7, 11, 8, 13, 6, 12, 7),
  Height = c(175, 160, 180, 163, 185, 155, 172, 158, 178, 162,
             188, 157, 183, 159, 177, 164, 190, 156, 181, 161)
)

shoes

write.csv(shoes, "shoesize.csv", row.names = FALSE)

## A dataframe named shoes was created containing the gender, shoe size, and height of 20 respondents.
```

```{r}
## b. Import the saved CSV into the R environment. Display the last 5 rows.

shoes <- read.csv("shoesize.csv")
tail(shoes, 5)

## The tail() function displays the last five rows of the imported shoe size dataset.
```

```{r}
## c. Describe the data by showing the structures and its content.

str(shoes)
head(shoes)

## The str() function displays the structure and data types of each column, while head() displays the first six rows of the dataset.
```

```{r}
## d. Inspect its dimensions. How many rows? How about columns?

dim(shoes)
nrow(shoes)
ncol(shoes)

## The dataset contains 20 rows and 3 columns. The rows represent the respondents, while the columns represent gender, shoe size, and height.
```

```{r}
## e. Inspect by using summary(). What is the difference of summary() from str() function?

summary(shoes)
str(shoes)

## The summary() function displays statistical information such as minimum, maximum, median, and mean for numerical columns. The str() function shows the columns and their data types.
```

```{r}
## f. Create a subset by males and females with their corresponding shoe size and height. What is its result?

male <- subset(shoes, Gender == "Male",
               select = c(ShoeSize, Height))
female <- subset(shoes, Gender == "Female",
                 select = c(ShoeSize, Height))

male
female

## The data is separated into two groups: male and female, with their corresponding shoe sizes and heights.
```

```{r}
## g. Find the mean of shoe size and height of the respondents.

mean(shoes$ShoeSize)
mean(shoes$Height)

## The average shoe size is 9.25, and the average height is 170,2 cm..
```

```{r}
## h. Is there a relationship between shoe size and height? Why?

plot(shoes$ShoeSize, shoes$Height,
     main = "Relationship Between Shoe Size and Height",
     xlab = "Shoe Size",
     ylab = "Height",
     pch = 19)

## Yes, there is a relationship between shoe size and height. People with larger shoe sizes tend to be taller.
```

```{r}
## Question 2

shoes$Gender <- factor(shoes$Gender)
shoes$Gender
levels(shoes$Gender)
str(shoes)

## Gender is now a factor with two categories:Female and Male.
```

```{r}
## Question 3

getwd()

## R uses the folder where the R Markdown file is saved. This helps R find the CSV file easily and other users can also run the file without changing folders.
```

```{r}
## Question 4: Checking the Structure of the Dataset

str(shoes)

## Gender is a factor, while ShoeSize and Height are numbers. If numbers are imported as text, R may not calculate the mean correctly. This can cause errors in the results.
```

```{r}
## Question 5

head(shoes)
tail(shoes)

## head() shows the first 6 rows, while tail() shows the last 6 rows. Checking both helps us see if the data was imported correctly. head() alone might miss errors or missing values at the end of the file.
```

```{r}
## Question 6
## a. Compute the correlation between shoe size and height across ALL observations.

cor(shoes$ShoeSize, shoes$Height)

## The correlation is 0.9924975.
## This means shoe size and height have a strong positive relationship.
```

```{r}
## b. Return all rows where ShoeSize is greater than or equal to 11, regardless of gender.

subset(shoes, ShoeSize >= 11)

## This displays all rows with a shoe size of 11 or higher.
## All the results are male students.
```

```{r}
## Question 7

# Separate male and female data
male <- subset(shoes, Gender == "Male")
female <- subset(shoes, Gender == "Female")

# Compute the mean height and shoe size
mean(male$Height)
mean(male$ShoeSize)

mean(female$Height)
mean(female$ShoeSize)

## Males have higher average height and shoe size than females.
## Gender may also affect the relationship between shoe size and height.
## We should study each gender separately for a clearer result.
```
